items.title: Domestic violence and psychological terror | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Domestic violence often goes hand-in-hand with psychological and emotional abuse. This documentary examines those mechanisms through the lens of what's known as "coercive control."

The term describes the many forms of everyday abuse of power and control that perpetrators use to systematically dominate the people they harm. Their methods range from constant surveillance and intimidation to threats of murder.

Excessive jealousy, isolation, humiliation, insults, GPS tracking, cyberbullying, financial dependence and threats of suicide or murder are typical forms of coercive control and central elements of domestic violence. Understanding this pattern changes the way a situation can be viewed. Instead of asking, "Why doesn't she just leave him?” the crucial question becomes, "What is he doing to prevent her from leaving?”

This documentary sets out to explore that. It looks at how abusive partners describe and justify their actions and how lawmakers and the justice system assess such behaviors. Among those interviewed are judges specialized in the area - like Gwenola Joly-Coz, First President of the Court of Appeal of Poitiers, and Ombeline Mahuzier, President of the Colmar Judicial Court.

Coercive control was first recognized explicitly as a mechanism of domestic violence in a 2023 French court case. This documentary traces the dynamics and stages of escalation in this complex system of abuse, which seeks to make women dependent through psychological violence and deprive them of basic freedoms. In the worst cases, that domestic terror ends in femicide.

Special structures have been established at courts that handle domestic violence cases in Poitiers, Colmar and Paris. With special permission, court proceedings there were filmed. Perpetrators gave their own accounts of events. Their statements are contrasted with assessments by judges, offering a rare insight into the mechanisms of domestic violence.

items.title: The paradox of Latino ICE agents
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>Under the second Trump administration, immigration enforcement agencies have undergone a significant expansion. President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill raised ICE’s budget from $10 billion to $85 billion, making it the most funded law enforcement agency in the United States. With that funding, they began offering economic incentives like signing bonuses and student loan forgiveness programs. The number of ICE agents and officers doubled in just one year, with another recruiting push underway through the end of 2026. 

Today, perhaps more than ever, the front lines of those federal immigration law enforcement agencies reflect the demographics of the populations they were created to police. Latinos are overrepresented in the Department of Homeland Security, which houses ICE and Border Patrol. Self-identified Latinos account for nearly half of Border Patrol agents and about 30 percent of ICE agents.

So why do so many Latinos join the immigration enforcement agencies that have targeted their own communities? The answers reveal complexities about American Latino identity and the splintered points of view on immigration policy at the border.

items.title: Space power struggle: Is a new space race looming? | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Space services have grown essential to our everyday lives: GPS, satellite internet and communications from orbit. Beyond civilian use, space systems are driving military conflict, fuelling a race for dominance in space.

The United States is planning a new missile defence system known as the 'Golden Dome.' In September 2026, it officially confirmed for the first time that it had already deployed weapons in orbit. China is rapidly expanding its own space program, working toward its own space ecosystem, including a lunar base. India, the United Arab Emirates, Russia and Europe are also investing into new missions and independent systems. Space has emerged as a strategic arena in the global struggle for power, with competition for influence and dominance extending far beyond nation states. Private companies control an ever-growing share of space infrastructure, led by Elon Musk's SpaceX and its Starlink satellite network.
The war in Ukraine offers a stark illustration of the geopolitical leverage that control over space infrastructure can provide. Since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, Starlink has become a central part of Ukraine's communications and defense. The coordination of military operations now depends, in part, on decisions made not by governments, but by a private company. Control of infrastructure in orbit translates into influence on Earth. At the same time, efforts to safeguard these critical systems are adding further momentum to the militarisation of space.

While space technology is advancing at unprecedented speed, the rules governing it belong to a very different era. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, adopted under the auspices of the United Nations, laid the foundation for international space law. It prohibits national claims of sovereignty over celestial bodies and the placement of weapons of mass destruction in orbit, but leaves many questions unresolved. Nearly six decades later, nations have yet to agree on a comprehensive framework of rules for this new space age.

The film takes viewers into a race that is already underway: a global struggle between nations, militaries and corporations for control of critical infrastructure, geopolitical influence and the rules that will shape our future in space — a place we're all increasingly dependent upon.

ABSTRACT
Many organizations still treat observability as a tooling decision: select a vendor, deploy agents, and expect insight to follow. Yet teams continue to struggle with fragmented signals, rising complexity, and slow incident response. The real issue is rarely the tool itself - it’s the absence of a shared foundation and a coherent product experience.

This talk reframes observability as an internal platform product, designed with clear users, sane defaults, and long-term evolution in mind. Drawing parallels to Kubernetes and platform engineering, we’ll explore why powerful primitives are not enough - and why standardization, correlation, and paved paths matter more than features.

We’ll look at how OpenTelemetry provides a vendor-neutral foundation for structured telemetry, decoupling instrumentation from backends and enabling correlation by default. This structured approach not only reduces cognitive load and improves reliability, it also lays the groundwork for AI-assisted debugging and natural language interaction with production systems.

Observability isn’t just about collecting more data. It’s about designing a platform that makes understanding systems easier - for both humans and machines.

ABSTRACT
"Jam-oriented programming" is the joke name of a new style of software development that is no joke at all. It adopts the practices and mentalities of an informal jam session to an extreme extent.

In a typical jam, there is no one in charge and anyone can make any sound they want at any time they choose. In jam-oriented programming, it's the same. Anyone can add, edit or delete code without any permission. Everyone is admin, nothing is certain and anything can happen. It sounds like chaos and it is. But it's also surprisingly successful, with entire music-making tools appearing overnight out of the multi-headed process and even a published academic paper to accompany it all.

How and why is this even possible? And what does it tell us about the way we collaborate as developers?

items.title: From the Netherlands to Colombia - Tanja's fight in the FARC | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>2001: Tanja Nijmeijer, a young woman from the Netherlands, went to Colombia as an English teacher. The social inequalities she found there left a deep impression on her. She became radicalized and joined the FARC guerrilla army.

Tanja first took up arms in the city, then later in the jungle. That was where the FARC - Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia - held out. For a long time family, friends and the public believed that she'd been the victim of a kidnapping; taken hostage, perhaps even already dead. Tanja soon became a key player within the FARC, in part because of her English skills.
She eventually took part as a member of the FARC delegation in peace negotiations with the government. To her supporters, she was a freedom fighter; to her opponents, a terrorist. She would become one of the most recognizable faces of a peace process that would ultimately end Latin America's longest war. With an international arrest warrant still out for her, Tanja remains unable to leave Colombia.
Filmmaker Marcel Mettelsiefen uses Tanja's personal story to trace a long, dark chapter in Colombia's recent history.
